1.1.1.heading: Q1.1 View A (1.5 marks)
1.1.1.context: The co-operative's planners want to know where each kind of vehicle is actually being picked up, so they can decide where to add parking bays.
1.1.1.text: (1) Create a view V_BUSIEST_BAYS that reports, for each body type, the single station at which vehicles of that body type have been collected the most times. The view should show the body type, the station name, and the number of collections, ordered from most collections to fewest. (1 mark) Hint: this is a "top item within each group" problem. Consider a window function such as RANK() or ROW_NUMBER() with a PARTITION BY clause, and use Common Table Expressions to build the query up in a semantically meaningful way.

1.2.heading: Q1.2 View B (1.5 marks)
1.2.text: Every charge a member incurs is ultimately billed to the account at the top of their sponsorship chain. A member with no sponsor pays their own charges. A sponsored member's charges pass to their sponsor — and if that sponsor is itself sponsored, the charges keep passing up the chain until they reach an account with no sponsor. Create a view V_ACCOUNT_LIABILITY that identifies the ten accounts liable for the largest total amount charged between 1 January 2026 and 30 June 2026 inclusive. The view should show the account's member id, member name, and the total amount billed to it. Hint: the chain can be more than one level deep, so an expression such as COALESCE(sponsor_id, member_id) will give the wrong answer. Consider a WITH RECURSIVE Common Table Expression.

1.3.3.text: (3) A member logs a large damage charge. Run the following statement, then re-run Query A and Query B and report what each returns. 3.2.heading: Q3.2 Suppressing scan types (4 marks)
3.2.text: PostgreSQL allows you to influence the query planner with runtime configuration parameters in psql. https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/runtime-config-query.html In this section we will suppress the use of several different scan types in order to compare queries. Suppressing plan types is not recommended for production, but is useful for understanding why one plan would be chosen over another. Report and explain the execution plan for the following two queries (C & D): 3. with both index and sequential scans enabled; 4. with index scans enabled and sequential scans suppressed; 5. with index scans suppressed and sequential scans enabled. Explain why the query planner might choose one method over another. You should refer to the reported times and costs from the execution plan, the number of rows fetched, your knowledge of query planning (and anything else you feel is relevant). Note: For this question, bitmap and index-only scans count as index scans too. The index IDX_EVENT_TYPE_TIME from Q2.1 should still be in place. Query C: SELECT * FROM BOOKING_EVENTS WHERE event_type < 'Collect'; Query D: SELECT * FROM BOOKING_EVENTS WHERE event_type >= 'Collect'; (2 marks for explaining up to 6 possible query plans; 2 marks for explaining the query planner's choices.) Between them, Queries C and D return every row of BOOKING_EVENTS exactly once — they differ only in which side of 'Collect' they take. Your explanation should account for why that is enough to change the plan. Be sure to reset index, bitmap, index-only and sequential scans back to on before proceeding to another question.

4.2.1.heading: Q4.2 Deadlock (3 marks)
4.2.1.context: In Q4.1 neither transaction could make progress on the other's terms, but only one of them was ever blocked. A deadlock is the symmetric case: two transactions each hold something the other is waiting for, so neither can move. Neither has done anything wrong on its own — it is the interleaving that traps them. Two staff are correcting odometer readings after a service run, and they work through the same two vehicles in opposite orders.

_q4_background.heading: Q4 Transactions (9 marks total)
_q4_background.text: In PostgreSQL, a transaction is set up by surrounding the SQL commands of the transaction with BEGIN and COMMIT commands. For example, a banking transaction would look like: BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100.00 WHERE name = 'Alice'; -- some more statements etc etc COMMIT; https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-transactions.html In this question we will examine what happens when two transactions occur concurrently. Background: how PostgreSQL reads You have seen two ways of keeping a concurrent schedule serialisable: locking protocols such as two-phase locking, and timestamp ordering. PostgreSQL uses neither of these for ordinary reads, so what you are about to observe will not follow from either one directly. This section gives you what you need; you are not expected to have met it before. Instead of taking read locks, a PostgreSQL query reads from a snapshot — a consistent picture of the database containing exactly those changes that were committed before the snapshot was taken. Because reading acquires no locks, readers never block writers and writers never block readers. At PostgreSQL's default isolation level, READ COMMITTED, a new snapshot is taken at the start of every statement. Two statements in the same transaction may therefore see different data, if another transaction committed in between them. Two consequences are worth holding on to as you work through this question: • A trigger runs inside the transaction that fired it. Any query the trigger makes is answered from that transaction's current snapshot. It gets no special or privileged view of the database. • A snapshot is not a lock. Reading a row records nothing and reserves nothing; it does not prevent another transaction from changing what you just read.
